source.title_on_document: The Roles of Idea Generation and Elaboration in Human-AI Collaborative Creativity

supplement.where: Appendices A to D are at the end of this PDF (pp. 32-34). No separate supplement is referenced. Data are on OSF: https://osf.io/nz6ag/?view_only=81c63168f1f64f62b2e865265b8ab343 (p. 8).
supplement.holds: Appendix A and B: screenshots of the AI-help and No-AI writing interfaces. Appendix C: prompt classification scheme. Appendix D: prompt-count correlations without outlier removal. All main statistics are in the main text.

paper_design_summary: 263 Penn State introductory psychology students (391 recruited) took part in an online study and each wrote two short stories (minimum 150 words, three-word prompt), one with free access to a GPT-3.5 chatbot (AI-help) and one without (No-AI). The order of the two conditions was randomized with equal numbers starting in each, and the two prompts were counterbalanced across conditions. Stories were scored for originality by an automated model (MAoSS) and for diversity contribution with sentence embeddings, and the two conditions were compared with paired t-tests.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the AI-help and No-AI story-writing conditions; the two three-word prompts were counterbalanced across conditions
assignment.quote: Participants completed two stories, with (AI-help) and without AI help (No-AI). The order of presentation was randomized, such that an equal number of participants completed the AI-help and No-AI conditions first.

arms.name: AI-help
arms.description: Wrote a story while chatting with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 via custom API) in a side textbox; system prompt limited output to bullet points and prevented full story passages; copy-paste disabled; told to use ChatGPT only as a 'source of ideas'.

arms.name: No-AI
arms.description: Same interface without the ChatGPT textbox; story textbox only.

participants.exclusions: 391 students recruited. Removed after participation: 68 who reported using external aid such as AI or internet (excluding the AI provided in the experiment), 53 who failed either of two attention checks, 7 who scored below 2.5 SD on any intelligence test. Final sample 263. The paper does not say how many of the 391 were assigned to each order, so no randomized count is recorded; within-person design, so the same 263 people appear in both arms.
participants.who: Students in an introductory psychology course at Pennsylvania State University; 235 female, 27 male, 3 other; mean age 18.9 (SD 2.17); 95 percent had used ChatGPT or another LLM chatbot before.
participants.quote: We recruited a total of 391 students enrolled in an introductory psychology course at Pennsylvania State University to take part in the online study. ... In total, our final sample consisted of 263 participants

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, GPT-3.5 base model called through a custom API with a hidden system prompt
ai_tool.how_used: Free chat in a textbox beside the story box. The hidden system prompt made the model act as a creativity support tool and restricted output to bullet points, with no full story passages. Copy-paste was disabled site-wide, and participants were told not to ask ChatGPT to write the story. A practice story task (50 words, 2 minutes) structured like the AI-help condition preceded both conditions.

task.description: Short story of at least 150 words using all three words of a prompt (pen-paper-write or year-week-embark), adapted from the five-sentence short-story task; instructed to 'use their imagination and be creative'.
task.duration: Instructed to spend at least 10 minutes per story (not enforced); submission blocked until 150 words.

outcomes.name: Story originality (MAoSS score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Multilingual Assessment of Short Stories (MAoSS), a fine-tuned LLM trained to predict human-rated originality; correlates with human ratings at r = .86 for English stories (p. 11). Scale 0-1. Partial correlations controlling for word-count difference are reported only for the mechanism analyses, not for the condition contrast.

contrasts.reported: Paired-samples t-test: AI-help M = .56, SD = 08 [printed without decimal point] vs No-AI M = .52, SD = 08; t(262) = 5.56, p < .001, d = .34, 95% CI [.021, .045]. N = 263 (abstract). The paper does not say whether d uses the SD of the paired differences or of the scores.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Results, Story Originality; p. 15, Figure 2 (left panel)

outcomes.name: Diversity contribution of each story
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Leave-one-out change in mean pairwise semantic distance (1 - cosine) of sentence embeddings; prompt words removed from stories before embedding. Positive score = removing the story decreases dataset diversity (the story adds diversity).

contrasts.reported: Paired-samples t-test: AI-help M = -.000026, SD = .00033 vs No-AI M = .000027, SD = .00034; t(262) = -1.99, p = .047, d = -.123, 95% CI [-0.0001, -0.0000006]. Higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal is needed.
contrasts.locator: p. 17, Results, Story Diversity; p. 15, Figure 2 (middle panel, values multiplied by 10^3)

diversity_detail.metric: Diversity contribution: overall dataset diversity (mean pairwise 1 - cosine distance over all story pairs) minus the same quantity with the story removed
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of stories within a prompt dataset (pen-paper-write or year-week-embark). The datasets are split by prompt, not by condition, so each dataset pools AI-help and No-AI stories; each story's score is its leave-one-out effect on that pooled dataset.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Paired-samples t-test over 263 participants' story-level scores (one story per condition per participant)
diversity_detail.notes: The paper does not report a per-condition set-level diversity (mean pairwise distance within AI-help stories vs within No-AI stories). Authors note the effect is smaller than in Doshi and Hauser (2024) and that the metric needs validation (p. 22).

company_involvement.description: No company authors or funders. Funding: NSF grants to R.E.B.; Aarhus University sources to J.R. (p. 1, Author Note). OpenAI's GPT-3.5 was used only as the tool.

eligibility.reason: Within-person design in which the order of AI-help and No-AI conditions was randomized (p. 9), which the codebook accepts. 263 people analyzed (p. 9). Originality is scored on the stories by an automated model and diversity by sentence embeddings (pp. 11-12). The abstract calls it a 'naturalistic study', but the design section states randomized order.

one_line_finding: Within the same 263 students, stories written with GPT-3.5 access scored higher on automated originality (.56 vs .52, t(262) = 5.56, d = .34) and had lower embedding-based diversity contribution (d = -.123, p = .047) than stories written without AI (pp. 14 and 17, Figure 2).
open_questions: The practice story task, done before both conditions, was 'structured in the same way as the AI-help condition' (p. 10), so all No-AI stories were written after some ChatGPT exposure; half were also written after the AI-help story. Order effects are not reported.
68 participants were removed after the task for self-reported use of external aid such as AI or internet (p. 8-9); the paper does not say in which condition, so exclusion may relate to treatment.

Diversity contribution is computed within prompt datasets that pool both conditions, not within each condition's set of stories; whether this matches the atlas's across_people measure needs a decision.
The number assigned to each order (out of 391 recruited) is not given; only 'an equal number' is stated.
notes: Not listed as outcomes: (1) self-assessed originality and its accuracy (self-report; Kendall tau AI-help .161, No-AI .195; multilevel interaction t(413) = -0.22, p = .83; self-assessment error AI-help M = 2.43, SD = 1.15 vs No-AI M = 2.14, SD = 1.18; pp. 17-18). (2) Correlational mechanism analyses within the AI arm: originality difference scores vs integration of AI responses (r = .13, p = .03), generation prompt count (r = .19, p = .002), elaboration prompt count (r = .02, p = .702); diversity difference scores unrelated to all three (pp. 14-17, Figure 3; Appendix D). These are not randomized contrasts. Participants also completed other creativity tasks and questionnaires 'not relevant to the research questions' (p. 9); no other paper using these participants is named. The originality SDs are printed as '08' (p. 14).
